core_condition: at least one measured effect recorded in observed_effects from Ventora telemetry or public corpora

evidence.rationale: Real but moderate and heavily moderated. Worchel, Lee & Adewole (1975) cookie study is the classic demonstration; Lynn (1991) provides a quantitative review of commodity-theory scarcity effects. The effect holds but depends strongly on type (limited-quantity vs limited-time), perceived cause (demand-caused stronger than supply-caused), and credibility. A recent meta-analysis in the corpus confirms a moderate, variable effect. Weaker and more context-dependent than loss aversion or framing — hence grade B and evidence score 2.

product_applicability.rationale: Directly implementable at conversion (limited quantity, real deadlines, capacity caps). Highly relevant to Ventora checkout/paywall. Reference: genuine product drops, cohort caps, and Booking.com as the canonical real-vs-fake example.

measurability.rationale: Maps to cvr, time_to_purchase, conversion_before_deadline — Amplitude-reachable and A/B-testable.

orthogonality.rationale: Substantial overlap: operates partly as loss-of-opportunity (hybrid with LA-01) and demand-caused scarcity shades into social proof (SP-08). Kept distinct because its driver is limited availability specifically. Score 2 reflects real, documented overlap.

safety.rationale: Tied with VR-02 for the highest-risk mechanism in the set. Fake scarcity — invented low-stock counts, resetting countdown timers, fake 'X viewing now' — is the single most common e-commerce dark pattern and is now explicitly illegal under EU UCPD/DSA and targeted by the FTC (Booking.com faced regulatory action). Score 1 is the honest flag: the mechanism is legitimate ONLY with genuine limits, and misuse is both trivially easy and specifically unlawful. Three block-severity hard rules (genuine_scarcity_only, no_fake_timers, no_manufactured_limits) plus the precondition gate (has_genuine_limit) are the mitigation. Any scarcity implementation gets the strictest review.

dissent: Beyond the moderation issues, scarcity has a well-documented backfire: when perceived as a manipulation tactic, it triggers reactance and reduces trust and intent — the opposite of the intended effect. Consumers are increasingly literate about fake-scarcity tactics, so the effect may be weakening in exactly the digital contexts we operate in. This, combined with the legal exposure of fake scarcity, is why SC-06 is admitted at the threshold minimum (total 11) with the strictest guardrails: it earns its place only for genuine limits, and its use should be conservative and measured rather than assumed effective. If our own measurement shows reactance/backfire in a niche, the mechanism is demoted for that context.

evidence_sources.ref: Worchel, Lee & Adewole (1975). Effects of supply and demand on ratings of object value. J Personality and Social Psychology 32(5).
Lynn (1991). Scarcity effects on value: A quantitative review of the commodity theory literature. Psychology & Marketing 8(1).

notes: Sources cross-checked against /corpora/evidence/SC-06.json (214 records; both prep pins had wrong/unresolved DOIs — corrected here: Worchel to 10.1037/0022-3514.32.5.906, Lynn review to 10.1002/mar.4220080204; both works arrived via term search, and a recent scarcity meta-analysis is present). Scored at threshold (11) by design — this is the weakest-evidence, highest-risk mechanism admitted so far; safety 1 is the honest flag. Verdict INCUBATING; CORE strictly on a measured effect; backfire/reactance in any niche triggers per-context demotion.
